questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'When we opened the gate, the neighbours ___ us about the noise.'

options.text: have warned
options.feedback: 'Have warned' is present perfect, and it points to a time that still matters now, not to a moment in the past.

options.text: were warning
options.feedback: 'Were warning' is past continuous, so it describes an action in progress rather than a finished earlier one.

options.text: had warned
options.feedback: 'Had warned' is past perfect: the warning was finished before the moment they opened the gate.

options.text: had warn
options.feedback: After 'had' the verb needs its past participle, and the participle of 'warn' is 'warned', not 'warn'.

questions.explanation: The past perfect is 'had' plus a past participle, and it places one finished action before another past action. Here the warning was already complete when the gate was opened.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct option: 'I ___ that film three times before Maria recommended it.'

options.text: have seen
options.feedback: 'Have seen' is the present perfect, and it points at the present rather than at a moment in the past.

options.text: had seen
options.feedback: 'Had seen' is the past perfect, so the three viewings sit entirely before Maria's later recommendation.

options.text: was seeing
options.feedback: 'Was seeing' is the past continuous and describes an action still in progress, not a finished count.

options.text: seen
options.feedback: 'Seen' is only a past participle on its own; it cannot open the sentence without an auxiliary verb.

questions.explanation: The past perfect is formed with 'had' plus a past participle and places a completed action earlier than another past action. Three viewings finished before the recommendation, so 'had seen' is the only correct form here.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'By the time the storm reached the coast, the fishermen ___ their boats to the harbour.' Which tense fits the blank?

options.text: already tied
options.feedback: 'Already tied' on its own gives no tense marker, so it never states when the tying happened.

options.text: had already tied
options.feedback: 'Had already tied' shows the tying was finished before the storm reached the coast.

options.text: are tying
options.feedback: 'Are tying' is the present continuous and belongs to the present, not to a past storm.

options.text: had already tie
options.feedback: 'Tie' is the base form, but the past perfect needs the past participle 'tied' after 'had'.

questions.explanation: The clause 'By the time the storm reached the coast' fixes a past moment, so the earlier action needs the past perfect. 'Had already tied' places the completed tying of the boats before that moment.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which form completes 'The team had ___ all the way to the coast before the storm reached us'?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: driven
options.feedback: 'Driven' is the past participle of 'drive', and it is exactly what the past perfect requires after 'had'.

options.text: drove
options.feedback: 'Drove' is the simple past form, so it cannot stand after the auxiliary 'had'.

options.text: drive
options.feedback: 'Drive' is the dictionary form, and the past perfect never takes a base verb after 'had'.

options.text: driving
options.feedback: 'Driving' is the present participle, which belongs to the continuous forms and not to the past perfect.

questions.explanation: Every past perfect has the same skeleton: the auxiliary 'had' followed by the past participle. The third form of 'drive' is 'driven', so 'had driven' is the complete and correct phrase.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence reports that the letter arrived before the ceremony began?
questions.context: English class in Santa Ana, SV.

options.text: By the time the ceremony began, the invitation had reached us.
options.feedback: 'Had reached' places the arrival of the letter before the start of the ceremony.

options.text: The invitation reached us after the ceremony ended, so we read it too late to attend.
options.feedback: 'After' points to a moment later than the ceremony, the opposite of what the question asks.

options.text: The invitation had reached us by the time the ceremony will begin.
options.feedback: 'Will begin' is a future form, so the reference moment is not in the past at all.

options.text: The invitation reached us by the time the ceremony was beginning.
options.feedback: 'Was beginning' makes the two actions overlap, and an overlapping action cannot come before the other one.

questions.explanation: The past perfect exists to place one finished action before another past action. 'By the time the ceremony began' sets a past reference point, so the arrival of the letter must be 'had reached'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'She ___ the keys before she realised the door was unlocked.' Which option completes the sentence correctly?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: was looking for
options.feedback: 'Was looking for' is the past continuous, which describes an action in progress rather than a finished search.

options.text: has found
options.feedback: 'Has found' is the present perfect, and it ties the action to the present instead of to an earlier past moment.

options.text: would find
options.feedback: 'Would find' is conditional, and a hypothetical result never states when the keys were actually found.

options.text: had found
options.feedback: 'Had found' is the past perfect, so the search was complete before she noticed the unlocked door.

questions.explanation: The past perfect, 'had' plus a past participle, marks an action finished before a second past action. Finding the keys came first, so 'had found' is the form the sentence needs.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'By the time the ambulance arrived, the nurse ___ the wound.'

options.text: was cleaning
options.feedback: 'Was cleaning' is the past continuous and puts the treatment in progress at the moment the ambulance arrived.

options.text: has already dressed
options.feedback: 'Has already dressed' is the present perfect, so it looks forward from now rather than back from an arrival.

options.text: will already dress
options.feedback: 'Will already dress' projects the action onto the future, so it says nothing about a treatment completed before the ambulance.

options.text: had already dressed
options.feedback: 'Had already dressed' shows the treatment was finished before the ambulance reached the scene.

questions.explanation: 'By the time' marks a past reference point, and anything completed before that point takes the past perfect. The wound was dressed earlier, so the correct auxiliary is 'had' plus the participle 'dressed'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'When the students reached the museum in San Salvador, the guide had already started the tour.' Which sequence matches the sentence?

options.text: The students arrived before the guide started the tour.
options.feedback: This reverses the sequence: the tour had already begun when the students arrived.

options.text: The guide started the tour before the students arrived.
options.feedback: The past perfect 'had already started' places the start of the tour before the students' arrival.

options.text: The guide started the tour at the exact moment the students arrived.
options.feedback: The word 'already' and the past perfect indicate an earlier event, not simultaneous actions.

options.text: The guide never started the tour.
options.feedback: The affirmative phrase 'had already started' confirms that the tour began.

questions.explanation: The past perfect identifies an action completed before another past event. Here, starting the tour precedes reaching the museum.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'When the ambulance reached the hospital, the doctors ___ waiting since noon.'

options.text: were already waiting
options.feedback: 'Were already waiting' is the past continuous, and it describes a situation in progress when the ambulance arrived.

options.text: wait
options.feedback: 'Wait' is the dictionary form, but an auxiliary is required here because the time reference lies in the past.

options.text: have been waiting
options.feedback: 'Have been waiting' is the present perfect continuous and belongs to the present, not to a past arrival.

options.text: had been waiting
options.feedback: 'Had been waiting' places the waiting that started at noon before the ambulance reached the hospital.

questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous joins the auxiliary 'had' with 'been' plus the -ing form, and it describes an activity that was already under way before another past moment. The doctors had been waiting since noon when the ambulance arrived.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence reports that the power failed before the family sat down to eat?

options.text: The lights went out just as we sat down to eat, so both events happened together.
options.feedback: 'Just as' makes the two actions simultaneous, and simultaneous events cannot be ordered by the past perfect.

options.text: The lights had gone out by the time we sat down to eat.
options.feedback: 'Had gone out' places the blackout earlier than the moment the family began eating.

options.text: The lights will have gone out by the time we sat down to eat.
options.feedback: 'Will have' belongs to the future perfect, and the reference moment here is in the past.

options.text: The lights had gone out when we will sit down to eat.
options.feedback: 'Will sit' is a future form, so the second action is not the past reference point the sentence needs.

questions.explanation: The past perfect is 'had' plus a past participle, and it places one completed action before another past action. A blackout finished before the meal began, so 'had gone out' is the only correct form.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'Andrea could not submit her application because she ___ the required certificate at home before leaving.'

options.text: has left
options.feedback: The present perfect connects an action to the present, whereas this sentence explains an earlier cause of a past problem.

options.text: had left
options.feedback: The past perfect places leaving the certificate before the failed attempt to submit the application.

options.text: had leave
options.feedback: After 'had', the past perfect requires the past participle 'left', not the base form 'leave'.

options.text: was leaving
options.feedback: The past continuous presents an action in progress, but the certificate had already been left at home.

questions.explanation: Use 'had left' to express the earlier completed action that caused Andrea's later difficulty.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: A student says, 'I had never used a microscope before that biology lesson.' What does this tell us about the student's experience?

options.text: The student refuses to use microscopes in future lessons.
options.feedback: The sentence describes experience before a past lesson; it expresses no future refusal.

options.text: The student had no experience using a microscope before the lesson.
options.feedback: 'Had never used' describes the absence of that experience up to the past reference point.

options.text: The student used microscopes regularly before the lesson.
options.feedback: 'Never' rules out any earlier experience with microscopes.

options.text: The student was using a microscope when the lesson began.
options.feedback: The sentence describes prior experience, not an action in progress when the lesson started.

questions.explanation: The negative past perfect describes something that had not happened before a specified past moment.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the sentence: 'The mechanic told us the battery ___ fail because of the heat.'
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: already started
options.feedback: 'Already started' carries no tense auxiliary, so it never states when the failure took place.

options.text: will start
options.feedback: 'Will start' projects the failure onto the future and leaves the earlier timeline unstated.

options.text: would already start
options.feedback: 'Would already start' is conditional and describes a hypothetical, not a real earlier failure.

options.text: had already started
options.feedback: 'Had already started' places the beginning of the failure before the moment the warning was spoken.

questions.explanation: In the past perfect, 'had' plus a past participle marks an action finished before another past action. The battery had already started to fail before the mechanic gave the warning, so the timeline runs in that order.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which form of 'write' correctly completes the past perfect sentence 'The class had ___ three drafts before submitting the essay'?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: written
options.feedback: 'Written' is the past participle of 'write', producing the correct form 'had written'.

options.text: wrote
options.feedback: 'Wrote' is the simple past form; the auxiliary 'had' requires a past participle.

options.text: writing
options.feedback: 'Writing' is the present participle and cannot directly complete 'had' in the past perfect.

options.text: write
options.feedback: 'Write' is the base form, whereas the past perfect requires the past participle.

questions.explanation: The past perfect consists of 'had' plus the past participle. The irregular participle of 'write' is 'written'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses the past perfect correctly?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: By the time the bell rang, the students had left the classroom.
options.feedback: 'Had left' is past perfect and places the departure earlier than the moment the bell rang.

options.text: By the time the bell rings, the students had left the classroom.
options.feedback: 'Rings' is the simple present, so it offers no past moment for the past perfect to precede.

options.text: By the time the bell rang, the students have left the classroom.
options.feedback: 'Have left' is the present perfect, which links the departure to the present instead of to the past bell.

options.text: By the time the bell rang, the students were leaving the classroom.
options.feedback: 'Were leaving' is the past continuous, which makes the two actions overlap rather than one preceding the other.

questions.explanation: The past perfect needs a completed earlier action and a past reference point. The bell rung in the past, and the leaving finished before it, so the auxiliary must be 'had' plus the participle 'left'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You want to ask whether Diego completed his homework before the electricity went out. Which question correctly uses the past perfect?

options.text: Did Diego had finished his homework before the electricity went out?
options.feedback: Past perfect questions use inversion with 'had'; they do not add the auxiliary 'did'.

options.text: Had Diego finished his homework before the electricity went out?
options.feedback: A past perfect question places 'had' before the subject and uses the past participle 'finished'.

options.text: Had Diego finish his homework before the electricity went out?
options.feedback: The auxiliary 'had' requires 'finished', not the base form 'finish'.

options.text: Has Diego finished his homework before the electricity went out?
options.feedback: 'Has finished' is present perfect, but the question asks about completion before another past event.

questions.explanation: Form a past perfect question with 'Had + subject + past participle'. This asks about completion before a past reference point.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'The trail was already flooded when the hikers reached the river.' What does the sentence tell us about the timeline?
questions.context: English class in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The flooding happened before the hikers reached the river.
options.feedback: 'Already flooded' presents the flood as finished before the arrival at the river.

options.text: The flooding happened after the hikers reached the river.
options.feedback: 'After' reverses the order, because the sentence states the trail was flooded when they got there.

options.text: The hikers and the flood happened at the same moment.
options.feedback: 'Already' rules out simultaneity: the flooding is finished before the hikers appear.

options.text: The trail never flooded at any point in the past.
options.feedback: The verb phrase is affirmative, so it confirms that the flooding did happen before the arrival.

questions.explanation: 'Already flooded' places a finished state before a second past action. The flooding was complete before the hikers got to the river, and that earlier timing is exactly what the sentence communicates.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Read: 'By the time the school announced the scholarship, Lucía had submitted her university application. She revised it the next morning.' Which conclusion is supported by the verb tenses and time expressions?

options.text: Lucía submitted her application because the scholarship announcement persuaded her.
options.feedback: Her submission preceded the announcement, so the announcement could not have prompted that earlier submission.

options.text: Lucía revised her application before submitting it for the first time.
options.feedback: The passage places the revision the next morning, after an application had already been submitted.

options.text: The school announced the scholarship only after Lucía revised her application.
options.feedback: The revision occurred the morning after the announcement, so this reverses their order.

options.text: Lucía's initial submission preceded the announcement, and her revision followed it.
options.feedback: 'Had submitted' establishes the earlier submission, while 'the next morning' places the revision after the announcement.

questions.explanation: The past perfect anchors the initial submission before the announcement. The explicit phrase 'the next morning' establishes the later revision.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which rule explains the position of 'never' in the sentence 'The team had never faced such a difficult opponent before the final'?

options.text: 'Never' replaces 'had' when the sentence is negative.
options.feedback: 'Had' remains necessary to form the past perfect; 'never' supplies the negative meaning.

options.text: 'Never' requires the past participle to become a base verb.
options.feedback: Adding 'never' does not change the verb form: the past perfect still requires 'faced'.

options.text: 'Never' must come immediately after the object 'opponent'.
options.feedback: Its standard position here is before 'faced', not after the object.

options.text: 'Never' normally goes between the auxiliary 'had' and the past participle.
options.feedback: The standard order is 'had + never + past participle', as in 'had never faced'.

questions.explanation: In the past perfect, 'never' normally appears after 'had' and before the past participle, without changing the tense structure.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly uses 'by the time' with the past perfect to show that the equipment check was complete before the experiment began?
questions.context: English class in San Miguel, SV.

options.text: By the time the experiment began, the students have checked the equipment.
options.feedback: 'Have checked' is present perfect and does not establish completion before the past event 'began'.

options.text: By the time the experiment began, the students had checked the equipment.
options.feedback: 'Had checked' correctly marks the equipment check as completed before the experiment began.

options.text: By the time the experiment began, the students had checking the equipment.
options.feedback: 'Had checking' is not a valid past perfect form; 'had' requires the participle 'checked'.

options.text: By the time the experiment began, the students had check the equipment.
options.feedback: 'Check' is a base verb, but the past perfect requires the past participle 'checked'.

questions.explanation: 'By the time' sets a past reference point. 'Had checked' expresses an action already completed by that point.
questions.subject: ingles
